metadata.file_name: Random Forests Approach for Causal Inference with Clustered Observational Data.pdf
metadata.title: Random Forests Approach for Causal Inference with Clustered Observational Data

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The empirical analysis uses TIMSS 2015 Korea Grade-8 student data (students nested within schools) and estimates treatment effects of private math lessons on math achievement. The authors explicitly state that they ignored sampling weights that would otherwise weigh each individual, and they did not incorporate sampling weights or multiple plausible values, so results are not intended to generalize beyond the TIMSS sample. Standard errors are estimated using cluster bootstrap sampling with 5000 replicates, which addresses clustering uncertainty but does not replace complex-survey weighting. Because the study uses causal ML estimators (Causal Forests) and parametric multilevel models for propensity/outcome components, the manuscript does not report any ILSA weight variable (e.g., TOTWGT/W_FSTUWT) being applied.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used TIMSS 2015 Korea Grade-8 data and analyzed it as a two-level structure (students nested within schools) because most schools selected one classroom (130 schools with one classroom; 20 with two). Treatment is private math lessons at the student level (1=received; 0=not). Excluded students with inconsistent responses across two private-lesson participation questions: those answering Yes to receiving private math lessons but “did not attend” for months, and those answering No to receiving lessons but providing a non-“did not attend” months response. Additionally excluded students missing 7 out of 12 covariates. The final analytic sample comprised 4943 students from 149 schools.

main_findings.dataset_used: TIMSS 2015 Korea Grade-8 Mathematics (private math lessons treatment; first plausible value of math achievement)
main_findings.performance_metrics: ATE point estimates (95% CIs reported qualitatively): unadjusted mean difference=66.88; IPW=27.67; MMW-S=33.88; DR IPW=32.96; DR MMW-S=29.58; Causal Forests (CF+Est.PS)=25.54 to CF+ID=30.30. Confidence intervals overlap; IPW widest CI; CF+Est.PS narrowest CI.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2015 Korea Grade-8 Mathematics the study leveraged father education level, books at home, math confidence, school disadvantage percentage, and discipline problems to estimate the average treatment effect of private math lessons on math achievement (PV1), finding that private math lessons had a positive effect with adjusted ATE estimates ranging from 25.54 to 33.88 depending on the estimator. This indicates that, after accounting for observed student and school covariates via multilevel propensity-score adjustments and causal forests, private math lessons are associated with higher math performance, though the study does not apply sampling weights and uses only a single plausible value, limiting population generalizability and precision.

data.outcome_summary: The paper studies causal inference with clustered observational data using Causal Forests modified for multilevel settings, and then applies the approach to TIMSS 2015 Korea Grade-8 mathematics. In the real-data analysis (students nested within schools), the treatment is whether students received private math lessons (assigned at the student level), and the outcome is the first plausible value of math achievement (each student has five PVs, but the study uses only PV1). The authors estimate ATEs using IPW, MMW-S, doubly robust (DR) estimators, and Causal Forests with multilevel propensity scores (and optionally cluster labels). The unadjusted mean difference was 66.88 points, reduced to 27.67 (IPW) and 33.88 (MMW-S), with DR estimates of 32.96 and 29.58; Causal Forests ranged from 25.54 to 30.30. Confidence intervals overlap across methods, with IPW producing the widest and CF+Est.PS the narrowest intervals. A key limitation is that sampling weights were ignored and multiple plausible values were not used, so results may not generalize to the full TIMSS target population.
